The curve $y=f(x)$ is shown above. At which of the following points is $f(x)$ continuous?

- $x=-2$
- $x=1$
- $x=3$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider each point separately.

- The function $f(x)$ is continuous at $-2.$ The graph can be drawn in the neighborhood of $x=-2$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

- The function $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=1.$ Since there is a jump at $x=1,$ it is impossible to draw the function in the neighborhood of $x=1$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

- Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is continuous $x=3.$ The graph can be drawn in the neighborhood of  $x=3$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

Hence, the correct answer is  "I and III only".

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Behavior of a Function in the Neighborhood of a Point
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13831128/assets/c132c73b7ca4759882959f9df42110c36e31f3c8af27afa02c0caa20f5f94d52.png)

Which of the following statements are true with respect to the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is plotted above. 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=1$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=f(1)$
- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$
questions.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. We have $f(1)=1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, from the graph we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x) & =1, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1=f(1).$

- Statement III is true. The graph of $f(x)$ can be drawn without taking our pencil off of the paper in the neighborhood of $x=1.$

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=1$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$ exists
- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$
questions.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is false. From the graph we can see that no value has been assigned to $f(x)$ at $x=1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x) & =1, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 
${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.$

- Statement III is false. The function is not even defined at $x=1.$ The graph contains a break at $x=1.$ It's impossible to draw the graph of $f(x)$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13831128/assets/1867a80955ae4b456cbcb011eefed96431f2b12926994942613eb947e55e38c6.png)

 

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$

- $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \, 2}f(x)$ exists

- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $f(2)=2.$

- Statement II is false. From the graph, we can see that the left and right-sided limits are different:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \, 2}f(x)$ does not exist.

- Statement III is false.  The graph of the function breaks at $x=2.$ It's impossible to draw the graph of $f(x)$ without taking our pencil off of the paper. Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x=2.$

In conclusion, only statement I is true.
